name: Access Control Lists
author: Recurse
subject: networking
description: Read wildcard masks, write standard, extended and named IPv4 ACLs, place and apply them, then verify and troubleshoot them.

lesson.intro: By default a router forwards every packet it has a route for. An access control list (ACL) gives it a rule book: permit this, deny that. ACLs are pure logic, which is why the exam loves them and why small mistakes break real networks. This lesson covers how a router reads an ACL, wildcard masks bit by bit and the range math the exam asks for, standard, extended and named ACLs, protocols, ports and ICMP, editing with sequence numbers, where to place them, and how to verify and troubleshoot them with the commands you will use on the job.
objectives: Predict the action an ACL takes on a packet using top-down, first-match logic and the implicit deny
Convert between prefix lengths, subnet masks, address ranges and wildcard masks
Configure standard, extended and named IPv4 ACLs with the right protocols and ports, edit them with sequence numbers and apply them to interfaces and vty lines
Choose the right router, interface and direction for an ACL
Verify ACLs with show commands and hit counters, and fix common ACL faults

sections.title: What an ACL does and how a router reads it
sections.body:
The guest VLAN (10.1.50.0/24) should reach the internet but never the server subnet (10.1.10.0/24). The router has routes to both, so without help it forwards guest traffic to the servers happily. An **access control list** is the help: an ordered list of `permit` and `deny` statements, each called an access control entry (ACE).

ACLs have two jobs. The obvious one is **packet filtering**: attach the ACL to an interface in a direction, and the router drops what the list denies. The other job is **classification**: features such as NAT, QoS, route filtering and vty access control use an ACL to select traffic, and there `permit` means "this matches" rather than "let it through."

The processing rules are short, and everything else follows from them:

- The router compares the packet with the lines **top down**, in order.
- The **first line that matches** decides the action, and the router stops looking. Lines further down are never checked for that packet.
- If no line matches, an invisible **implicit deny any** at the end drops the packet. You never type it and it never appears in the configuration.

Two consequences come up constantly. An ACL with only `deny` lines blocks everything, because whatever the denies miss falls into the implicit deny. And an ACL with only `permit` lines still blocks everything you did not list.

Direction matters too. An **inbound** ACL checks packets as they enter the interface, before the routing decision. An **outbound** ACL checks packets after routing, as they leave. Each interface can have at most **one ACL per direction per protocol** (one IPv4 ACL in, one out). Finally, an outbound ACL never filters packets the router creates itself, such as its own pings or routing updates.
sections.code:
Packet arrives on an interface with an ACL applied in that direction

  line 10 matches?  yes -> take its action (permit = forward, deny = drop). STOP.
                    no  -> next line
  line 20 matches?  yes -> take its action. STOP.
                    no  -> next line
  ...
  no line matched   -> implicit "deny any": drop (no counter, no log)

activity.title: First match wins
activity.prompt: Build a two-line list: deny one host, then permit any. Send a test packet from that host and one from its neighbor, and watch which line catches each. Then remove the permit line and send the neighbor's packet again: nothing you wrote matches it, so the implicit deny drops it. Finally swap the order of two lines and see how the result changes.

sections.pitfall: Forgetting the implicit deny. If you write only deny lines to block one subnet, you have actually blocked everyone; add a permit for the traffic that should pass.

check.question: ACL 5 contains a single line, access-list 5 deny 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255, and is applied inbound on an interface. What happens to a packet from 10.2.2.2 arriving on that interface?
choices: It is permitted because it does not match the deny line
It is denied by the implicit deny at the end of the list
It is permitted because standard ACLs permit by default
It is logged and then forwarded
check.explanation: The packet does not match the only configured line, so it reaches the end of the list and the implicit deny drops it. An ACL with no permit statements blocks all traffic.

sections.title: Wildcard masks, bit by bit
sections.body:
ACLs match addresses with an address plus a **wildcard mask**. The wildcard looks like a subnet mask but works the other way around, one bit at a time:

- A **0** bit means "this bit must match the address in the ACL."
- A **1** bit means "ignore this bit" (it is wild).

So `10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255` means the first three octets must be exactly 10.1.1 and the last octet can be anything: every address in 10.1.1.0/24.

For a whole subnet there is a shortcut: **wildcard = 255.255.255.255 minus the subnet mask**, octet by octet. A /26 mask is 255.255.255.192, so its wildcard is 0.0.0.63. A /20 mask is 255.255.240.0, so its wildcard is 0.0.15.255. A /30 gives 0.0.0.3.

To find what an address-and-wildcard pair matches, the address is the low end of the range and the address plus the wildcard is the high end, as long as the wildcard is one of these contiguous values. `172.16.32.0 0.0.15.255` matches 172.16.32.0 through 172.16.47.255, because 32 + 15 = 47.

Two keywords save typing. `host 10.1.1.5` means `10.1.1.5 0.0.0.0` (match exactly one address). `any` means `0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255` (match everything).

IOS also tidies up what you type: where a wildcard octet is 255, it sets that octet of the address to 0. Type `access-list 21 permit 10.1.1.1 0.0.255.255` and the configuration shows `10.1.0.0 0.0.255.255`. Wildcards do not have to be contiguous (for example 0.0.254.255 matches only even third octets), but you will rarely need that outside of puzzles.
sections.code:
Goal: match 172.16.32.0/20   mask 255.255.240.0   wildcard 0.0.15.255

                 third octet in binary
ACL address  32  0010 0000
wildcard     15  0000 1111     0 = must match, 1 = ignore
                 ^^^^ these four bits must stay 0010

matching third octets: 0010 0000 (32) up to 0010 1111 (47)
result: 172.16.32.0 through 172.16.47.255

host 10.1.1.5   =  10.1.1.5 0.0.0.0
any             =  0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255
sections.tip: Sanity check any wildcard by adding it to the address: the result should be the subnet's broadcast address.
sections.pitfall: Typing a subnet mask where a wildcard belongs. access-list 5 permit 10.1.1.0 255.255.255.0 does not match 10.1.1.0/24; it ignores the first three octets and matches any address whose last octet is 0.

check.question: Which wildcard mask matches every address in a /27 subnet?
check.explanation: A /27 mask is 255.255.255.224, and 255 minus 224 is 31, so the wildcard is 0.0.0.31. 255.255.255.224 is the subnet mask itself, and 0.0.0.63 would match a /26.

sections.title: Wildcard math: ranges and quick checks
sections.body:
Exam questions turn wildcards around in three ways: they give you a range and ask for the ACL entry, give you an entry and ask which addresses match, or ask whether one address is matched. All three rest on one fact: a contiguous wildcard always describes a block whose size is a power of 2, and the block starts on a multiple of its size, exactly like a subnet.

**From a range to an entry.** Hosts 10.1.8.0 through 10.1.15.255 span 8 values in the third octet (8 to 15). A block of 8 means a wildcard of 7 in that octet, and 8 is a multiple of 8, so the entry is `10.1.8.0 0.0.7.255`. Hosts 192.168.1.16 to 192.168.1.31 are a block of 16 starting at 16: `192.168.1.16 0.0.0.15`. If a range is not a power of 2 or does not start on a multiple of its size, such as .10 to .20, no single entry covers it exactly and you need several lines, as shown below.

**From an entry to a range.** In the octet where the wildcard is neither 0 nor 255, the block size is the wildcard plus 1. The address is the low end of the block and the address plus the wildcard is the high end: `172.16.48.0 0.0.3.255` covers 172.16.48.0 to 172.16.51.255. Matching is bit by bit, so an entry typed as `172.16.50.0 0.0.3.255` still matches 48 through 51, because the two low bits of the octet are ignored. Always write the low end of the block so the ACL reads the way it behaves.

**Quick membership check.** Is 10.1.13.77 matched by `10.1.8.0 0.0.7.255`? The third octet's block runs from 8 to 15 and 13 is inside, so yes. 10.1.16.1 is not, because 16 starts the next block.

**Several subnets in one line.** Neighboring subnets that together form one aligned block can share an entry: 10.1.4.0/24 through 10.1.7.0/24 is `10.1.4.0 0.0.3.255`. 10.1.5.0/24 through 10.1.8.0/24 is also four subnets, but it does not start on a multiple of 4, so it needs more than one line.
sections.code:
Range 10.1.8.0 to 10.1.15.255
  third octet 8..15 = 8 values = block of 8   ->  wildcard 7
  8 is a multiple of 8                        ->  10.1.8.0 0.0.7.255

Range 192.168.1.16 to 192.168.1.31
  16 values starting at 16                    ->  192.168.1.16 0.0.0.15

Range 192.168.1.10 to 192.168.1.20
  11 values, not a power of 2                 ->  several lines:
  192.168.1.10 0.0.0.1    matches 10 and 11
  192.168.1.12 0.0.0.3    matches 12 to 15
  192.168.1.16 0.0.0.3    matches 16 to 19
  host 192.168.1.20       matches 20

activity.title: Blocks and wildcards
activity.prompt: Work through the drill, and for every subnet also write its ACL entry: the network address plus a wildcard of block size minus 1 in the interesting octet. Check yourself by adding the wildcard to the address: you should land on the broadcast address the drill expects.

sections.pitfall: Writing an entry for a range that is not an aligned power-of-2 block. 192.168.1.10 0.0.0.15 does not mean .10 to .25; it matches .0 to .15, because the low four bits are ignored entirely.

check.question: Which single ACL entry matches exactly the addresses 172.20.32.0 through 172.20.63.255?
check.explanation: 32 to 63 is 32 values in the third octet, a block of 32, so the wildcard octet is 31, and 32 is a multiple of 32. 0.0.63.255 would cover 0 to 63, and 0.0.15.255 only 32 to 47.

sections.title: Standard numbered ACLs
sections.body:
A **standard ACL** can match only one thing: the packet's **source IP address**. That makes it simple and limited.

Standard numbered ACLs use numbers **1 to 99** and **1300 to 1999** (the second range was added when 99 ran out). You build them with the global command `access-list number {permit | deny} source [wildcard]`, one line at a time, and IOS adds each new line to the end in the order you type them. `access-list number remark text` adds a comment that stays with the ACL. Because these are global commands, the prompt stays at `R1(config)#`.

An ACL does nothing until you apply it. Under the interface, `ip access-group number {in | out}` attaches it in one direction.

The example below is the scenario from the console lab: hosts in 192.168.20.0/24 must not reach the LAN behind G0/1, and everyone else may. The deny line catches the blocked subnet. The `permit any` line is what keeps every other source working; without it, the implicit deny would cut off the whole LAN. The ACL is applied **outbound** on G0/1, the interface toward the protected LAN, so it only affects traffic heading to that LAN. That placement choice is explained in the placement section.
sections.code:
R1(config)# access-list 10 remark Keep the 192.168.20.0/24 hosts off the G0/1 LAN
R1(config)# access-list 10 deny 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255
R1(config)# access-list 10 permit any
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip access-group 10 out

activity.title: Standard ACL: block one subnet
activity.prompt: Build ACL 10 so it denies 192.168.20.0/24 and permits everyone else, then apply it outbound on G0/1. Before you add the permit line, run show access-lists and predict what the list would do on its own. Notice that the access-list commands keep you in global configuration mode.

sections.pitfall: Expecting a standard ACL to filter by destination. It sees only the source address, so a line written with a server's address matches packets coming from that server, not going to it.

check.question: Which ACL number creates a standard numbered IPv4 ACL?
check.explanation: Standard numbered ACLs use 1 to 99 and 1300 to 1999, so 1500 is standard. 150 and 199 are in the extended range 100 to 199, and 2100 is in the extended range 2000 to 2699.

sections.title: Extended numbered ACLs
sections.body:
A standard ACL cannot say "block guests from the web server but let them use everything else." An **extended ACL** can, because it matches much more of the packet: the **protocol**, the **source** and **destination** addresses, and for TCP and UDP the **source and destination ports**. Extended numbered ACLs use **100 to 199** and **2000 to 2699**.

The general form is `access-list number {permit | deny} protocol source wildcard [operator port] destination wildcard [operator port]`. The protocol can be `ip` (every IPv4 packet), `tcp`, `udp`, `icmp`, or others such as `ospf`, `gre` and `esp`. A packet matches a line only if **every** field on that line matches.

Ports take an **operator**: `eq` (equal), `neq` (not equal), `lt` (less than), `gt` (greater than) or `range low high`. **Where** you write the port matters. A port written after the source address matches the **source** port; a port written after the destination address matches the **destination** port. Client applications use random high source ports, so to match traffic going to a web server, the `eq 80` goes after the destination. IOS also shows well-known ports by name: `eq 80` displays as `eq www`, 23 as `telnet`, 21 as `ftp`, 25 as `smtp` and 53 as `domain`.

The next section lists the protocol keywords, port numbers and ICMP options you will meet most, along with the `established` and `log` keywords.

The example is the console lab's goal: the 192.168.1.0/24 LAN may browse the web, and nothing else. Notice what the implicit deny now blocks: DNS, ping, SSH, everything not on these two lines.
sections.code:
R1(config)# access-list 100 permit tcp 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 80
R1(config)# access-list 100 permit tcp 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 443
R1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip access-group 100 in
!
! Source 192.168.1.0/24, any destination, destination port 80 or 443.
! Everything else arriving on G0/1 hits the implicit deny.

activity.title: Extended ACL: web only
activity.prompt: Write ACL 100 so the 192.168.1.0/24 LAN can reach any web server on TCP 80 and 443, then apply it inbound on G0/1, the LAN-facing interface. When the checks pass, look at show access-lists and ask yourself: can these users still resolve names with DNS? Which single line would you add, and where?

sections.pitfall: Putting the port after the source address. access-list 101 permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 eq 443 any matches packets whose source port is 443, which describes replies from HTTPS servers, not requests from your clients.

check.question: Which packets match: access-list 101 permit tcp any eq 80 host 10.1.1.10 ?
choices: TCP packets from any host to web server 10.1.1.10 on port 80
TCP packets from 10.1.1.10 to any web server
All TCP traffic to 10.1.1.10
TCP packets from web servers (source port 80) to host 10.1.1.10
check.explanation: eq 80 follows the source (any), so it matches the source port. These are packets coming from web servers back to 10.1.1.10. To match requests to a server at 10.1.1.10, eq 80 would go after the destination.

sections.title: Matching protocols, ports and ICMP
sections.body:
An extended ACL line names a protocol first, and that choice decides what else the line can match.

- `ip` matches every IPv4 packet. Use it when only the addresses matter, as in `deny ip 10.1.50.0 0.0.0.255 10.1.10.0 0.0.0.255`.
- `tcp` and `udp` add the port operators (`eq`, `neq`, `lt`, `gt`, `range`). You can only match a port after naming the protocol that carries it, and you must pick the right one: DNS queries are UDP 53, SSH is TCP 22, TFTP is UDP 69.
- `icmp` adds message types: `echo` (a ping request), `echo-reply`, `unreachable` and `time-exceeded`, which traceroute relies on.
- Other protocols are matched by keyword or number and have no ports: `ospf` (IP protocol 89), `eigrp` (88), `gre` (47), `esp` (50) and `ahp` (51, for AH).

Two keywords tune TCP lines. `established` matches only TCP segments that have the ACK or RST flag set. Every segment of an open connection except the client's very first SYN carries ACK, so `permit tcp any 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 established`, inbound on the internet link, lets replies to inside users' connections back in while blocking connections started from outside. It is a simple stateless trick; a stateful firewall does the same job properly. The `log` keyword sends a syslog message when the line matches, which is most useful on a final `deny ip any any log`.

Know the common ports by number and by the keyword IOS displays in `show access-lists` (table below). Some services need more than one entry: DNS uses UDP 53 for most queries and TCP 53 for large replies and zone transfers, and DHCP uses UDP 67 toward the server and UDP 68 toward the client.
sections.code:
Port    Transport  Service   Shown by IOS as
20, 21  TCP        FTP       ftp-data, ftp
22      TCP        SSH       22
23      TCP        Telnet    telnet
25      TCP        SMTP      smtp
53      UDP, TCP   DNS       domain
67, 68  UDP        DHCP      bootps, bootpc
69      UDP        TFTP      tftp
80      TCP        HTTP      www
110     TCP        POP3      pop3
123     UDP        NTP       ntp
161     UDP        SNMP      snmp
443     TCP        HTTPS     443
514     UDP        Syslog    syslog

IP protocols with no ports: ospf 89, eigrp 88, gre 47, esp 50, ahp 51
sections.pitfall: Matching a service with the wrong transport. permit tcp ... eq 53 alone leaves most DNS queries (UDP) blocked, and permit udp ... eq 22 never matches SSH.

check.question: An inbound ACL on the internet interface contains permit tcp any 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 established. Which segments does this line match?
choices: Only SYN segments from internet hosts
TCP segments with the ACK or RST flag set, such as replies to connections that inside users opened
All UDP replies to inside hosts
Every TCP segment sent to 10.1.1.0/24
check.explanation: established matches segments with ACK or RST set. An outside host's first SYN has neither, so new inbound connections fall through to the next lines, while replies to inside users match.

sections.title: Named ACLs, sequence numbers and editing
sections.body:
Number 117 tells you nothing six months later; a name such as GUEST-IN tells you everything. **Named ACLs** use the same matching logic as numbered ones, created with `ip access-list standard NAME` or `ip access-list extended NAME`. That command moves you into ACL configuration mode (`R1(config-std-nacl)#` or `R1(config-ext-nacl)#`), where you type the `permit`, `deny` and `remark` lines without the `access-list number` prefix. You apply a named ACL with the same `ip access-group NAME in|out`.

In ACL mode every line gets a **sequence number**. IOS numbers them 10, 20, 30 and so on unless you give one. Sequence numbers make editing easy:

- `no 20` deletes just the line with sequence 20.
- `15 deny host 10.1.1.9` inserts a new line between 10 and 20.
- A line typed without a number goes to the end.

The same editing works for numbered ACLs if you enter them with `ip access-list standard 24` or `ip access-list extended 101`. The traditional global `access-list` command can only append to the end, and IOS still saves numbered ACLs in the running configuration as global `access-list` lines, whichever way you created them.

If the gaps run out, `ip access-list resequence NAME 10 10` renumbers the list. And before rebuilding a large ACL that is in use, a safe habit is to remove it from the interface first (`no ip access-group`), edit, verify, then reapply, so the interface is never filtering with a half-built list.
sections.code:
R1(config)# ip access-list extended WEB-ONLY
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 80
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 443
R1(config-ext-nacl)# do show ip access-lists WEB-ONLY
Extended IP access list WEB-ONLY
    10 permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq www
    20 permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 443
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 15 permit udp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.1.10.53 eq 53
R1(config-ext-nacl)# no 20
R1(config-ext-nacl)# do show ip access-lists WEB-ONLY
Extended IP access list WEB-ONLY
    10 permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq www
    15 permit udp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.1.10.53 eq domain
sections.pitfall: Typing no access-list 101 to remove one line. For numbered ACLs that command deletes the entire list, and an interface that still references a missing ACL filters nothing at all.

check.question: An extended named ACL has lines 10 and 20. In ACL configuration mode, how do you add a new line that is checked between them?
choices: Type the line normally; IOS sorts lines by specificity
Type the line with sequence number 15 in front of it
Delete the ACL and rebuild it in the new order
Use the insert-before 20 keyword
check.explanation: Lines are checked in sequence-number order, so 15 lands between 10 and 20. A line without a number goes to the end of the list, and IOS never reorders extended ACL lines for you.

sections.title: Placement and direction
sections.body:
Writing the right lines is half the job; the other half is choosing the router, the interface and the direction.

**Direction** is always from the router's point of view. `in` means packets entering the router through that interface. `out` means packets leaving the router through that interface. Trace the packet's path, then ask which interface it crosses and which way.

Cisco's placement rules, which the exam expects you to know:

- Place **extended ACLs as close to the source** as possible. They match precisely (source, destination, protocol, port), so filtering early drops unwanted traffic before it wastes bandwidth across the network, without collateral damage.
- Place **standard ACLs as close to the destination** as possible. They match only the source address, so a standard deny near the source would block that source from reaching everything, not just the one destination you cared about.

Take the topology below. The goal is to stop Host A's subnet (10.1.1.0/24) from reaching the server subnet (10.3.3.0/24) while still reaching everything else.

- With an **extended** ACL, filter on R1 G0/0 inbound, the first interface the traffic enters: `deny ip 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 10.3.3.0 0.0.0.255`, then `permit ip any any`.
- With a **standard** ACL, filter on R3 G0/1 outbound, toward the servers: `deny 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255`, then `permit any`. The same standard ACL placed on R1 G0/0 inbound would cut Host A's subnet off from everything.

Remember the limit of one IPv4 ACL per interface per direction: a second `ip access-group` command for the same direction replaces the first. An inbound ACL also saves the router work, because denied packets are dropped before the routing lookup.
sections.code:
10.1.1.0/24                                                        10.3.3.0/24
Host A --[G0/0] R1 [G0/1]----[G0/0] R2 [G0/1]----[G0/0] R3 [G0/1]-- Servers
            ^                                                 ^
   extended ACL here, inbound                     standard ACL here, outbound
   (close to the source)                          (close to the destination)
sections.pitfall: Applying an ACL in the wrong direction. An ACL that matches source 10.1.1.0/24 does nothing outbound on the 10.1.1.0/24 LAN interface, because packets leaving toward that LAN are coming from somewhere else.

check.question: Why does Cisco recommend placing standard ACLs close to the destination?
choices: Standard ACLs can only be applied outbound
Standard ACLs match only the source address, so near the source they would block traffic to every destination
Standard ACLs use more CPU near the source
Routers near the source cannot process wildcard masks
check.explanation: A standard ACL cannot distinguish destinations. Filtering close to the destination limits its effect to traffic headed there. Standard ACLs can be applied in either direction.

sections.title: Verifying ACLs and filtering vty access
sections.body:
Three commands answer almost every ACL question on a live router.

- `show access-lists` lists every ACL (IPv4 and others, such as IPv6), and `show ip access-lists [name | number]` shows IPv4 ACLs only. Both list each line with its sequence number and a **match counter**. Counters are the fastest way to see which line is catching traffic. There is no counter for the implicit deny; if you want to count or log what falls off the end, add an explicit `deny ip any any log` as the last line. `clear access-list counters` resets the counters before a test.
- `show ip interface type number` shows which ACL is applied to the interface and in which direction (`Outgoing access list is ...`, `Inbound access list is ...`).
- `show running-config` (or `| include access-group`) confirms both the ACL lines and where they are applied.

ACLs also protect the router itself. Telnet and SSH sessions arrive on the **vty lines**, and the line subcommand `access-class` applies a standard ACL to them. `access-class 5 in` means only sources permitted by ACL 5 may open a session to the router, no matter which interface the session arrives on. Users who are filtered never even see a login prompt. (The `out` keyword filters sessions that users start from the router to other devices, and is rarely used.)
sections.code:
R1# show ip access-lists
Standard IP access list 10
    10 deny   192.168.20.0, wildcard bits 0.0.0.255 (57 matches)
    20 permit any (1432 matches)
Extended IP access list 100
    10 permit tcp 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq www (380 matches)
    20 permit tcp 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 443 (2211 matches)
R1# show ip interface GigabitEthernet0/1 | include access list
  Outgoing access list is 10
  Inbound  access list is 100
!
R1(config)# access-list 5 permit 10.10.99.0 0.0.0.255
R1(config)# line vty 0 15
R1(config-line)# access-class 5 in
sections.pitfall: Using ip access-group under the vty lines. Lines take access-class; ip access-group is an interface command.

check.question: Which command shows whether an ACL is applied to G0/1 and in which direction?
choices: show access-lists
show ip interface GigabitEthernet0/1
show interfaces status
show ip route
check.explanation: show ip interface lists the inbound and outbound ACLs for the interface. show access-lists displays the ACL contents and counters but not where they are applied.

sections.title: Troubleshooting ACLs
sections.body:
When an ACL misbehaves, work through it in the same order every time instead of rewriting lines at random.

1. **Is it applied, where you think?** `show ip interface` for the interface and direction. Right router, right interface, right direction?
2. **Does the ACL exist?** An interface can reference an ACL name that was never created (often a typo). A missing ACL filters nothing, so all traffic passes.
3. **Which line is matching?** Read top down and check the counters. A broad line above a specific one steals its matches; a specific line with zero matches is often sitting below a broader one.
4. **Are the wildcards right?** Add the wildcard to the address and confirm the range.
5. **For extended ACLs**: are source and destination in the right order? Is each port on the correct side? Is the protocol right (DNS queries use UDP 53, SSH uses TCP 22)?
6. **What is the implicit deny catching?** The traffic you forgot: DNS, DHCP, ICMP, and above all **routing protocols**. An inbound ACL that permits only web traffic also drops OSPF hellos (IP protocol 89), and the neighbor goes down when the dead timer expires. Add `permit ospf any any` near the top.
7. **Outbound and the router's own packets**: outbound ACLs do not filter traffic the router itself generates, so testing with a ping from the router can mislead you. Test from a host.

The example below shows step 6 in action. The fix is a single inserted line, `5 permit ospf any any`, not removing the ACL.
sections.code:
R2# show ip access-lists BRANCH-IN
Extended IP access list BRANCH-IN
    10 permit tcp 10.2.2.0 0.0.0.255 any eq www (1022 matches)
    20 permit tcp 10.2.2.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 443 (5310 matches)
R2# show ip interface GigabitEthernet0/1 | include Inbound
  Inbound  access list is BRANCH-IN
%OSPF-5-ADJCHG: Process 1, Nbr 3.3.3.3 on GigabitEthernet0/1 from FULL to DOWN, Neighbor Down: Dead timer expired

activity.title: Troubleshoot: everything is blocked
activity.prompt: This router starts broken: an ACL meant to block one subnet is blocking all traffic. Before changing anything, run show access-lists and show running-config and explain to yourself exactly why every packet is dropped. Then fix it so the blocked subnet stays blocked and everyone else gets through.

sections.pitfall: Fixing an ACL problem by removing the ACL. It restores connectivity and silently removes the security the ACL was there to provide; find the missing or misplaced line instead.

check.question: In the example output, why did the OSPF neighbor on G0/1 go down after BRANCH-IN was applied inbound?
choices: OSPF hellos (IP protocol 89) match no line and are dropped by the implicit deny
Extended ACLs disable multicast on the interface
The ACL's web traffic used up the interface bandwidth
OSPF requires ACLs to be applied outbound only
check.explanation: Only TCP 80 and 443 are permitted, so the neighbor's incoming OSPF hellos fall into the implicit deny. After the dead interval with no hellos, the adjacency drops. Permitting OSPF at the top fixes it.

keyTerms.definition: Access control entry: one permit or deny line in an ACL.
A router checks ACL lines top down and applies the action of the first line that matches, ignoring the rest.
The invisible deny any at the end of every ACL that drops packets matching no configured line.
A 32-bit mask where 0 bits must match the ACL address and 1 bits are ignored; for a subnet it is 255.255.255.255 minus the subnet mask.
An ACL that matches only the source IPv4 address; numbered 1 to 99 and 1300 to 1999.
An ACL that matches protocol, source and destination addresses and ports; numbered 100 to 199 and 2000 to 2699.
An ACL identified by a name and configured in ACL mode with ip access-list standard or extended.
The number in front of each ACL line that sets its order and allows deleting or inserting single lines.
Interface subcommand that applies an ACL inbound or outbound.
Line subcommand that applies an ACL to vty lines to control who can open Telnet or SSH sessions to the device.
The number of values a contiguous wildcard covers in its interesting octet: the wildcard value plus 1, always a power of 2.
The eq, neq, lt, gt or range keyword that matches a TCP or UDP port; its position decides source or destination port.
Extended ACL keyword that matches TCP segments with the ACK or RST flag set, meaning traffic of a connection already open.
Command that lists IPv4 ACL lines with sequence numbers and per-line match counters.

summary: ACLs are read top down, the first matching line wins, and an implicit deny any drops whatever matches no line.
Wildcard 0 bits must match and 1 bits are ignored; for a subnet the wildcard is 255.255.255.255 minus the mask, and a range needs an aligned power-of-2 block to fit one line.
Standard ACLs (1-99, 1300-1999) match source only; extended ACLs (100-199, 2000-2699) match protocol, addresses and ports, with port position deciding source or destination.
Pick the right protocol for each port (DNS is mostly UDP 53, SSH is TCP 22), match routing protocols such as ospf by keyword, and use established for simple return traffic.
Named ACLs and sequence numbers let you delete (no 20) and insert (15 ...) single lines; extended ACLs go near the source, standard near the destination, one per interface per direction.
Verify with show ip access-lists counters and show ip interface; when traffic breaks, check application, existence, order, wildcards, ports and what the implicit deny catches.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a coworker how a router processes a packet against an ACL, why an ACL with only deny statements blocks everything, and how you would choose between a standard and an extended ACL and decide where to apply each one.

questions.question: A packet matches line 20 and also line 40 of an ACL. Which action does the router take?
choices: The action of line 40, because later lines override earlier ones
The action of line 20, because the first match wins
Deny, because conflicting matches are always denied
Permit, because a packet that matches twice is trusted
questions.explanation: The router stops at the first matching line and applies its action. Line 40 is never checked for that packet.

questions.question: ACL 1 below is applied inbound. Packets arrive from 10.1.1.5, 10.1.1.77 and 10.9.9.9. What happens to each?
questions.code:
access-list 1 deny host 10.1.1.5
access-list 1 permit 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255
access-list 1 deny 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255
access-list 1 permit any
choices: 10.1.1.5 denied, 10.1.1.77 permitted, 10.9.9.9 denied
10.1.1.5 permitted, 10.1.1.77 permitted, 10.9.9.9 denied
All three are denied by line 3
10.1.1.5 denied, 10.1.1.77 denied, 10.9.9.9 permitted
questions.explanation: 10.1.1.5 matches line 1 (deny). 10.1.1.77 misses line 1 and matches line 2 (permit). 10.9.9.9 misses lines 1 and 2 and matches line 3 (deny). Line 4 only catches sources outside 10.0.0.0/8.

questions.question: An engineer applies an ACL that contains only two deny statements, one for each of two problem hosts. What is the result?
choices: Only the two hosts are blocked
Nothing is blocked until a permit is added
All traffic through that interface and direction is blocked
The router rejects the ACL because it has no permit
questions.explanation: Every other packet matches neither deny and falls to the implicit deny, so everything is blocked. A permit any (or permit ip any any) at the end is needed.

questions.question: Besides filtering packets on an interface, which two jobs can an ACL do on a Cisco router? (Choose two.)
choices: Select which inside addresses NAT translates
Control which sources may open Telnet or SSH sessions to the router
Assign IP addresses to DHCP clients
Elect the STP root bridge
Tag frames with a VLAN ID
questions.explanation: ACLs classify traffic for features such as NAT and are applied to vty lines with access-class. DHCP addressing, STP elections and VLAN tagging do not use ACLs.

questions.question: R1 has ACL 30 (access-list 30 deny any) applied outbound on G0/1. An engineer runs ping from R1 itself to a host out G0/1, and it succeeds. Why?
choices: Ping uses ICMP, which standard ACLs cannot match
Outbound ACLs do not filter packets that the router generates itself
ACLs only take effect after the router reloads
The implicit deny only applies inbound
questions.explanation: An outbound ACL filters packets the router routes, not packets it originates, such as its own pings and routing updates. Testing from a host behind the router would show the ACL working.

questions.question: What is the implicit deny, and what does it mean for an ACL that contains only permit statements?
questions.answer: Every ACL ends with an invisible deny any that drops any packet matching no configured line. An ACL with only permit statements therefore still blocks everything it does not explicitly permit.
questions.explanation: The implicit deny never appears in the configuration and has no counter, which is why it surprises people.

questions.question: In an ACL wildcard mask, what does a 0 bit mean?
choices: The corresponding address bit is ignored
The packet is denied
The bit is part of the host portion
The corresponding address bit must match
questions.explanation: 0 means the bit must match the ACL address; 1 means ignore it. This is the reverse of how people often read subnet masks.

questions.question: What wildcard mask matches all addresses in a /26 subnet?
questions.explanation: A /26 mask is 255.255.255.192. 255 minus 192 is 63, so the wildcard is 0.0.0.63.

questions.question: What wildcard mask matches the subnet whose mask is 255.255.240.0?
Which range of addresses does 172.16.32.0 0.0.15.255 match?
questions.explanation: The third octet's low four bits are wild, so it can range from 32 to 32 + 15 = 47, with the last octet fully wild. That is 172.16.32.0/20.

questions.question: Which address is matched by the ACL entry permit 192.168.4.0 0.0.3.255 ?
questions.explanation: The wildcard 0.0.3.255 lets the third octet vary from 4 to 7 and the last octet be anything, so the range is 192.168.4.0 to 192.168.7.255. Only 192.168.7.200 falls inside it.

questions.question: Which addresses does the entry permit 10.1.0.0 0.0.254.255 match?
choices: Every address from 10.1.0.0 to 10.1.254.255
Addresses 10.1.x.y where the third octet x is an even number
Addresses 10.1.x.y where the third octet x is an odd number
Only addresses in 10.1.0.0/24
questions.explanation: 254 is 11111110 in binary, so only the lowest bit of the third octet must match the ACL address. That bit is 0 in 10.1.0.0, so the third octet must be even. This is a non-contiguous wildcard.

questions.question: An engineer meant to permit 10.1.1.0/24 but typed: access-list 5 permit 10.1.1.0 255.255.255.0 . What does this line actually match?
choices: Any IPv4 address whose last octet is 0
Exactly the 10.1.1.0/24 subnet
Only the single address 10.1.1.0
Nothing; IOS rejects the command
questions.explanation: Read as a wildcard, 255.255.255.0 ignores the first three octets and requires the last octet to equal 0. IOS accepts it (it displays as 0.0.0.0, wildcard bits 255.255.255.0), and it matches addresses such as 10.1.1.0, 172.16.5.0 and 192.168.9.0.

questions.question: Match each ACL address form to what it matches.
questions.explanation: host and any are shorthand for the all-zeros and all-ones wildcards. For contiguous wildcards, the range runs from the address to the address plus the wildcard.

questions.question: An engineer enters the command below. What does show ip access-lists display for this line?
choices: 10 permit 10.1.1.1, wildcard bits 0.0.255.255
10 permit 10.1.0.0, wildcard bits 0.0.255.255
10 permit host 10.1.1.1
An error, because the address does not match the wildcard
questions.explanation: IOS accepts the command but zeroes the address octets that the wildcard ignores, so 10.1.1.1 becomes 10.1.0.0. The match is the same either way.

questions.question: Which two number ranges identify standard numbered IPv4 ACLs? (Choose two.)
choices: 1 to 99
questions.explanation: Standard ACLs use 1-99 and 1300-1999. Extended ACLs use 100-199 and 2000-2699.

questions.question: You are in interface configuration mode for G0/1. Type the command that applies ACL 10 to packets leaving the router through this interface.
questions.explanation: ip access-group attaches an ACL to an interface, and out means packets exiting the interface after routing.

questions.question: Type the global command that adds a line to standard ACL 15 denying the single host 10.1.1.99.
questions.explanation: host 10.1.1.99 is shorthand for 10.1.1.99 0.0.0.0. In a standard ACL, a bare address with no wildcard is also treated as a host match.

questions.question: The goal is to stop the 10.1.1.0/24 users from reaching server 10.3.3.10, while allowing everything else. The engineer applies this standard ACL outbound on the interface toward the server. What is wrong?
questions.code:
access-list 20 deny host 10.3.3.10
access-list 20 permit any
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip access-group 20 out
choices: The permit any must come before the deny
Standard ACLs cannot use the host keyword
The ACL must be applied inbound, not outbound
A standard ACL matches only the source, so this line matches packets from the server, not to it
questions.explanation: Standard ACLs look only at the source address. Packets heading to 10.3.3.10 have source 10.1.1.x, so the deny never matches them. The line should deny 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 (or use an extended ACL that names both).

questions.question: Which field of a packet can a standard IPv4 ACL match?
choices: Destination IP address
Destination TCP port
Protocol number
Source IP address
questions.explanation: Standard ACLs match only the source IP. Destination, ports and protocol require an extended ACL.

questions.question: Which two number ranges identify extended numbered IPv4 ACLs? (Choose two.)
choices: 1 to 99
questions.explanation: Extended ACLs use 100-199 and the expanded range 2000-2699. 1-99 and 1300-1999 are standard.

questions.question: Complete the line so hosts in 10.1.1.0/24 may send email to the SMTP server 10.9.9.25.
choices: eq 25
eq 23
gt 25
eq 110
questions.explanation: SMTP is TCP port 25, and the operator follows the destination so it matches the destination port. 23 is Telnet, 110 is POP3, and gt 25 would match every port above 25 but not 25 itself.

questions.question: Users in 10.1.1.0/24 can resolve names but cannot open the HTTPS site on 172.16.5.5. ACL 150 is applied inbound on their LAN interface. What is wrong?
questions.code:
R1# show ip access-lists 150
Extended IP access list 150
    10 permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 eq 443 host 172.16.5.5
    20 permit udp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 172.16.5.53 eq domain (88 matches)
choices: HTTPS uses UDP, so line 10 needs udp instead of tcp
Line 10 checks source port 443; the clients use random source ports, so eq 443 belongs after the destination
Line 20 must come before line 10
The wildcard 0.0.0.255 is wrong for a /24
questions.explanation: eq 443 sits after the source, so it matches packets whose source port is 443, which client requests never have. Rewriting it as permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 172.16.5.5 eq 443 matches the destination port.

questions.question: Type one global command that adds a line to extended ACL 130 denying Telnet from any host in 10.1.1.0/24 to any destination.
accept: access-list 130 deny tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq telnet
questions.explanation: Telnet is TCP port 23, matched as the destination port, so eq 23 goes after the destination any. IOS will display it as eq telnet.

questions.question: IOS displays some port numbers by name in ACLs. Match each keyword to its port.
questions.explanation: Knowing these keywords lets you read show access-lists output, which uses the names even when you typed numbers.

questions.question: ACL 140 below is applied inbound on R1's internet-facing interface. What effect does it have?
questions.code:
access-list 140 deny icmp any any echo
access-list 140 permit ip any any
choices: Blocks all ICMP, including replies to inside users' pings
Blocks ping requests arriving from the internet, while other traffic, including echo replies, is permitted
Blocks all traffic, because ICMP lines disable the permit
Permits everything, because echo is not a valid keyword
questions.explanation: echo matches ICMP echo requests only. Outside hosts cannot ping in, but replies to pings sent by inside users (echo-reply) still match the permit ip any any.

questions.question: After entering ip access-list extended GUEST-IN, which prompt does IOS show?
choices: R1(config-if)#
R1(config-acl)#
R1(config-ext-nacl)#
R1(config-std-nacl)#
questions.explanation: Extended named ACLs use config-ext-nacl mode; standard named ACLs use config-std-nacl.

questions.question: You are in configuration mode for a named ACL. Type the command that deletes only the line with sequence number 20.
questions.explanation: In ACL configuration mode, no followed by a sequence number removes just that line. The rest of the ACL is untouched.

questions.question: Given the ACL below, an engineer types deny ip host 10.1.1.9 any in ACL mode without a sequence number. Where does the new line go, and is that a problem?
questions.code:
R1# show ip access-lists EDGE
Extended IP access list EDGE
    10 permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq www
    20 permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 443
    30 permit ip any any
choices: It becomes line 5 and works as intended
It replaces line 30
IOS sorts it into the most specific position automatically
It becomes line 40, after permit ip any any, so it never matches anything
questions.explanation: A line without a sequence number goes to the end. Line 30 permits everything first, so the new deny is never reached. Entering it as 5 deny ip host 10.1.1.9 any would put it at the top.

questions.question: Numbered ACL 101 is applied inbound on G0/0. An engineer enters no access-list 101 to remove one bad line, intending to retype it. What is the immediate effect on traffic arriving on G0/0?
choices: All traffic is permitted, because the interface now references an ACL that does not exist
All traffic is denied by the implicit deny
Only the bad line is removed; the others keep filtering
The interface shuts down until the ACL is recreated
questions.explanation: no access-list 101 deletes the whole ACL. The ip access-group 101 in command remains, but an empty or missing ACL filters nothing, so everything passes until lines are added again.

questions.question: Put the steps in a safe order for rebuilding a large ACL that is currently applied to a busy interface.
items: Remove the ACL from the interface with no ip access-group
Edit or rebuild the ACL lines
Check the result with show ip access-lists
Reapply the ACL with ip access-group
questions.explanation: Detaching first means the interface never filters with a half-built list. Verifying before reapplying catches ordering and wildcard mistakes.

questions.question: According to Cisco's guidelines, where should an extended ACL be placed?
choices: As close to the source of the traffic as possible
As close to the destination as possible
Only on the router's internet interface
On every router along the path
questions.explanation: Extended ACLs match precisely, so filtering near the source drops unwanted packets early without blocking other traffic.

questions.question: Using the topology below, you must stop 10.1.1.0/24 from reaching 10.3.3.0/24 with an extended ACL while allowing all other traffic. Where should it be applied?
choices: R3 G0/1 inbound
R1 G0/1 inbound
R1 G0/0 inbound
R3 G0/0 outbound
questions.explanation: Host A's packets first enter R1 on G0/0, so applying the extended ACL inbound there drops them at the earliest point. R1 G0/1 inbound would see traffic coming back from R2, and R3 G0/1 inbound sees traffic from the servers.

questions.question: An ACL that matches source 10.1.1.0/24 is applied outbound on R1 G0/0, the interface whose LAN is 10.1.1.0/24. The engineer expects it to stop those hosts from reaching other subnets. What actually happens?
choices: It works, because direction does not matter for standard ACLs
It has no effect on those hosts, because their packets enter G0/0 rather than leave through it
It blocks the hosts from reaching their default gateway only
IOS rejects the command because the subnets overlap
questions.explanation: Packets from the LAN enter R1 on G0/0, so an outbound ACL there never sees them. Outbound on G0/0 sees packets heading to the LAN, whose source is some other subnet.

questions.question: Interface G0/0 already has ip access-group 101 in. The engineer then enters ip access-group 102 in on the same interface. What is the result?
choices: Both ACLs are checked, 101 first
Both ACLs are checked, 102 first
ACL 102 replaces ACL 101 for inbound traffic
IOS rejects the second command
questions.explanation: Only one IPv4 ACL can be applied per interface per direction. The new command replaces the old one.

questions.question: Which command shows the lines of every IPv4 ACL along with how many packets each line has matched?
choices: show ip interface brief
show running-config interface
show ip access-lists
show ip route
questions.explanation: show ip access-lists (and show access-lists) list each ACL's lines with sequence numbers and match counters.

questions.question: You are in line vty 0 15 configuration mode. Type the command that allows only sources permitted by ACL 5 to open Telnet or SSH sessions to the router.
questions.explanation: access-class applies an ACL to the vty lines. in filters sessions coming into the router. ip access-group is for interfaces, not lines.

questions.question: A troubleshooter wants to see how many packets the end of an ACL is dropping, but the implicit deny has no counter. What can be done?
choices: Run show ip access-lists implicit
Enable debug ip packet on the interface permanently
Apply the ACL in both directions
Add an explicit deny ip any any log as the final line
questions.explanation: An explicit final deny does what the implicit deny would do, but it has a match counter and, with log, produces syslog messages.

questions.question: Based on the output below, which statement is true?
questions.code:
R1# show ip interface GigabitEthernet0/2 | include access list
  Outgoing access list is not set
  Inbound  access list is MGMT-ONLY
R1# show ip access-lists MGMT-ONLY
Standard IP access list MGMT-ONLY
    10 permit 10.10.99.0, wildcard bits 0.0.0.255 (842 matches)
choices: Packets entering G0/2 from outside 10.10.99.0/24 are dropped
Packets leaving G0/2 are filtered by MGMT-ONLY
MGMT-ONLY permits all traffic because it has no deny line
MGMT-ONLY applies only to Telnet and SSH sessions
questions.explanation: MGMT-ONLY is applied inbound and permits only 10.10.99.0/24; every other source falls into the implicit deny. Nothing is applied outbound, and as an interface ACL it filters all IPv4 traffic, not just remote logins.

questions.question: Host 10.1.1.66 can still Telnet anywhere even though ACL 120 below is applied inbound on its LAN interface. What is the best fix?
questions.code:
R1# show ip access-lists 120
Extended IP access list 120
    10 permit ip 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any (4210 matches)
    20 deny tcp host 10.1.1.66 any eq telnet
    30 deny ip any any (12 matches)
choices: Change line 20 to deny ip host 10.1.1.66 any
Apply ACL 120 outbound instead
Move the deny above the permit, for example as 5 deny tcp host 10.1.1.66 any eq telnet, and remove line 20
Delete line 30 so the implicit deny takes over
questions.explanation: Line 10 matches all of 10.1.1.0/24 first, so line 20 is never reached (zero matches). Specific lines must come before broader ones. Changing line 20's contents does not help while it sits below line 10.

questions.question: Guest users can still reach the servers. Based on the output below, why?
questions.code:
R1# show running-config interface GigabitEthernet0/0
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.1.50.1 255.255.255.0
 ip access-group BLOCK-GUEST in
R1# show ip access-lists
Extended IP access list BLOCK-GEUST
    10 deny ip 10.1.50.0 0.0.0.255 10.1.10.0 0.0.0.255
    20 permit ip any any
choices: The deny line needs a log keyword to take effect
The ACL should be applied outbound
The wildcard 0.0.0.255 is wrong for the guest subnet
The interface references BLOCK-GUEST, but the ACL was created as BLOCK-GEUST, so no ACL is filtering
questions.explanation: The names differ by a typo. An interface that points at an ACL that does not exist filters nothing, so all traffic passes. Fix the name in one place or the other.

questions.question: After BRANCH-IN is applied inbound on G0/1, web traffic works but the OSPF neighbor on G0/1 drops and stays down. Which change fixes it while keeping the filter?
questions.code:
ip access-list extended BRANCH-IN
 10 permit tcp 10.2.2.0 0.0.0.255 any eq www
 20 permit tcp 10.2.2.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 443
choices: Add 5 permit ospf any any to BRANCH-IN
Apply BRANCH-IN outbound instead
Add 30 permit tcp any any eq 89
Change the OSPF network type to point-to-point
questions.explanation: OSPF is IP protocol 89, not a TCP port. Its hellos match neither line and hit the implicit deny. permit ospf any any near the top lets them in without opening anything else.

questions.question: This ACL is applied inbound on the interface facing the 10.1.1.0/24 LAN. It should stop that LAN from reaching the web server 10.3.3.10 and allow everything else, but web access still works. Which line is wrong?
questions.code:
ip access-list extended NO-WEB
 10 deny tcp host 10.3.3.10 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 eq 80
 20 permit ip any any
choices: Line 20, because permit ip any any overrides every deny
Line 10, because source and destination are swapped; it should be deny tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.3.3.10 eq 80
Line 10, because eq 80 should be eq 443
Line 20, because it should be permit tcp any any
questions.explanation: Traffic from the LAN has source 10.1.1.x and destination 10.3.3.10. Line 10 lists them the other way around, so it never matches and line 20 permits the requests.

questions.question: Users behind an inbound extended ACL can no longer browse by name, though browsing by IP address works. The ACL permits only TCP 80 and 443. Which two additions are most likely needed? (Choose two.)
choices: permit udp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 53
permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 53
permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 23
permit icmp any any echo
permit udp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 69
questions.explanation: Name resolution is DNS on port 53, mostly UDP with TCP for large responses. Telnet (23), ping and TFTP (69) have nothing to do with resolving names.

questions.question: List the checks you would make, in order, when an ACL is not doing what it should.
questions.answer: Confirm it is applied to the right interface and direction (show ip interface); confirm the referenced ACL exists; read it top down with the hit counters to see which line matches; check wildcards; for extended ACLs check source and destination order, port position and protocol; finally consider what the implicit deny is catching, such as DNS or routing protocols.
questions.explanation: Working in a fixed order avoids rewriting lines that were never the problem.

questions.question: Type the wildcard mask for one ACL entry, 10.20.64.0 plus the wildcard, that matches exactly the addresses 10.20.64.0 through 10.20.127.255.
questions.explanation: 64 to 127 is 64 values in the third octet, a block of 64 that starts on a multiple of 64, so that octet of the wildcard is 63 and the last octet is fully wild: 0.0.63.255.

questions.question: Which line, applied inbound on the internet interface, lets web replies reach inside users in 10.1.1.0/24 but does not let an outside host open a new connection to an inside web server?
choices: permit tcp any 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 eq 80
permit tcp any eq 80 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 established
permit ip any any
permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 80
questions.explanation: Replies from web servers have source port 80 and the ACK flag set, so they match. An outside host's first SYN has no ACK, so established rejects it. The first option admits new connections to inside port 80, and the last option describes outbound requests, which never arrive inbound on this interface.
